c.v: This stage gives the bench a second scenario, one that cuts the supervisor's own input mid-route and judges how it responds. The relay's drop service fires while the robot is driving, and five checks decide what counts as a good reaction: that the cue actually went out, that the robot was really driving beforehand, how long and how far it took to come to rest, and that it was moving again once odometry returned.

The decision worth defending is that no single check is enough. A robot already standing still, or turning on the spot with zero forward speed, would pass a bare stop check for the wrong reason, and a cue that never fired at all would leave every later check unmeasured, which has to fail loudly rather than pass quietly. Checking that the robot was driving before the cue is what rules the first two cases out.
What we can now show:
./run_scenario.sh missing_odom

passes five times in a row, with its stop and distance limits tightened from those runs against the supervisor's own predicted numbers. And it fails two different ways on purpose, each naming a different cause: a drop shorter than the supervisor's timeout correctly changes nothing, while raising that timeout past the drop length makes the robot drive straight through, failing the stop checks while the route's own checks still pass.
By the end of this session,
bench_core
can judge a run in which odometry went away and came back, with GoogleTest tests that you wrote first and saw fail.
The pieces are all here. The relay drops
/odom
for a stretch of time when its service is called, the supervisor stops the robot when odometry is stale, and the runner watches the robot on
/odom_raw
, which the relay never touches. What is missing is the rule that says whether the bench behaved, and it has to be more careful than it first looks.

The obvious check is that the robot stopped. On its own it passes for the wrong reasons. A robot that was already standing still when the cue went out stops trivially. A robot turning on the spot has a forward speed of zero, so it reads as stopped while it is still moving. And a robot that stops and never starts again has also failed, in the other direction: the point of a drop with a length is that the bench recovers. So the scenario asks five things:

items.v: the cue went out at all, with the simulated time it went out at;
the robot was driving in the second before the cue, above
it was driving again after the drop ended.

c.v: The third and fourth are the same event measured two ways, and both are worth having. The time is the one to compare with the supervisor's arithmetic, and the distance is the one a person cares about: a robot that takes an extra 200 ms to stop matters because of the extra 4 cm.

The numbers come from the supervisor topic. After the last odometry message the supervisor's 20 Hz timer notices within 250 to 300 ms, the DiffDrive system brakes at 1 m/s² which takes 0.2 s from 0.2 m/s, and
/odom_raw

shows it up to one odometry period of 33 ms later: about 0.53 s, and about 8 cm at 0.2 m/s. The limits below are 1.50 s and 0.25 m, roughly three times each, so a busy machine doesn't turn a pass into a failure. Build 3 measures the real numbers and tightens them.

c.v: The three verdicts are the three outcomes worth telling apart. The first is the bench working. The second is a supervisor that never noticed, and it fails on the two checks that describe the stop while the others pass, so the report names the supervisor rather than the run. The third is a cue that never went out, where every check is unmeasured: nothing was tested, and a scenario that tested nothing must fail rather than pass quietly.
first_rest

at_rest_since

from the smoke scenario is a backward one, and the difference is the question each answers. The smoke scenario asks whether the robot ended the run at rest, so it looks at the trailing stretch. Here the robot stops in the middle and drives on, so the question is when it first came to rest after the cue, and the trailing search would find the end of the run or nothing at all. Both are in
bench/scenario.hpp
with names that say which is which.

By the end of this session,
./run_scenario.sh missing_odom
drives the route, cuts odometry partway through, and writes a verdict that covers both the route and the stop.
The runner gains one job: it fires the relay's drop service at a chosen moment and records the simulated time it went out. Three details in that sentence do the work.

The cue's time is measured from the first odometry message, the same zero the plan uses, so the scenario's timetable and its cue are on one clock. The cue is spent only when the relay's service is actually there, checked with
service_is_ready()
before
due()
is asked: a cue thrown at a service that discovery hasn't found yet would be lost, and the run would report a stop that never had a chance to happen. And the request is sent with
async_send_request
and a callback. Waiting for the reply inside the timer callback would deadlock, because the executor that has to deliver the reply is the one stuck in the wait.
The route's own checks come first and the stop's are appended, so one verdict says both whether the bench recovered and whether it finished the job. That is the reason
judge
took a list of checks rather than a fixed set: a scenario is the route plus whatever else it does to the robot.
scenario_runner
now uses a service interface, so it leaves the shared
foreach
in
src/bench_nodes/CMakeLists.txt

target_link_libraries
